title: Analytic Continuation, Monodromy, and Riemann Surfaces

items.title: Holomorphic germs at a point
Holomorphic germs at a point form a local ring
items.strategy: Use the neighborhood-agreement relation to define representatives, then apply the published holomorphic algebra rules to show sums, products, and reciprocals are representative-independent wherever the value at the base point is nonzero.

items.title: Function elements and direct analytic continuation
Analytic continuation along a path by admissible chains
Two admissible continuation chains along one path admit a common refinement
items.strategy: Pull back the function-element neighborhoods to an open cover of the compact interval and choose a Lebesgue subdivision fine enough that every subinterval lies inside one member of each chain.

items.title: The terminal germ of a continuation along a fixed path is chain-independent
items.strategy: Refine two admissible chains to a common subdivision and compare the successive representatives on each overlap; the identity theorem propagates the local agreements to the final germ.

items.title: Analytic continuation along a fixed path is unique whenever it exists
items.strategy: Any two continuations of the same initial germ along the same path determine two admissible chains, so the chain-independence theorem forces their terminal germs to agree.

items.title: The complete analytic function generated by one germ
Fixed-endpoint homotopic paths give the same analytic continuation
items.strategy: Subdivide the homotopy square by a Lebesgue grid so that each small square stays inside one function-element neighborhood, then propagate the continuation across adjacent grid edges until the two endpoint paths are compared.

items.title: On a simply connected domain, pathwise continuation glues to one holomorphic function
items.strategy: Compare any two paths from the base point to a target by concatenating one with the reverse of the other; trivial fundamental group makes that loop nullhomotopic, so monodromy removes the path ambiguity.

items.title: The monodromy corollary agrees with the earlier simply connected logarithm theorems
The germ space of a complete analytic function
The germ neighborhoods form a Hausdorff, second-countable Riemann-surface atlas
items.strategy: Take the neighborhoods coming from function elements as basic sets and verify the basis condition directly. Separate distinct germs by shrinking representatives and invoking the identity theorem, then build a countable atlas from rational discs reached by polygonal continuations.

items.title: The germ projection is a local biholomorphism
items.strategy: On each basic germ neighborhood, the projection is literally the chosen representative-domain chart map, so its inverse is holomorphic on that neighborhood and the local models patch compatibly.

items.title: A germ projection is not automatically a covering map
The Riemann surface of the logarithm is the complex plane over the punctured plane via exp
items.strategy: Start from the principal logarithm on the slit plane, continue it around loops in the punctured plane, and identify the resulting branches by the integer monodromy of the argument. The parameter on the resulting surface is exactly the logarithm value, so the projection becomes the exponential map.

items.title: The Riemann surface of an nth root is the n-sheeted covering w maps to w to the nth power
items.strategy: Use the slit-plane root branch as the local model and compare branches by their logarithms. The resulting germ surface is the finite quotient of the logarithm surface obtained by period n, and the projection is the power map.

items.title: Schwarz reflection is an analytic continuation construction
Singular boundary points and natural boundaries of function elements
A power series of finite radius has a singular point on its circle of convergence
items.strategy: Assume every boundary point is regular. Compactness of the boundary circle then gives finitely many continuation discs, which glue with the original series to a holomorphic function on a larger centered disc; the Taylor expansion at the center and the coefficient formula then contradict the original finite radius.

items.title: Pringsheim's theorem for power series with nonnegative coefficients
items.strategy: If the positive boundary point were regular, the Taylor expansion there would control the function on a larger real interval beyond the radius. Nonnegative coefficients make the majorization one-sided on the positive real axis, forcing a larger radius than allowed.

items.title: The factorial-gap series has the unit circle as a natural boundary
items.strategy: The published factorial-gap example gives radius one, Pringsheim makes 1 singular, and rotating by a root of unity changes the tail only by a polynomial. Every root of unity is therefore singular, and density on the unit circle forces a natural boundary.

title: Analytic Continuation, Monodromy, and Riemann Surfaces — Examples

items.title: Continuing the logarithm once around the unit circle adds 2 pi i
Continuing a square root once around the origin changes its sign
The logarithm surface admits the standard helicoid model
The square-root surface is a two-sheeted covering of the punctured plane
The geometric series has only one singular point on its unit circle
The factorial-gap series shows that a holomorphic function need not continue past its boundary
The series sum z to the n over n squared is continuous on the closed disc but singular at 1
FALSE: every holomorphic function on a domain continues past its boundary
FALSE: continuation along two paths with the same endpoints always agrees
FALSE: the Riemann surface of a multivalued function is automatically a subset of C squared
FALSE: every boundary point of a radius-one power series is singular
